metaTitle: Dubai to Abu Dhabi Day Trip With a Private Driver Guide
metaDescription: How to see the Grand Mosque, the Louvre and Qasr Al Watan in one day from Dubai with a private driver: drive time, the best order of stops, tolls and costs.

content:
A day trip from Dubai to Abu Dhabi with a private driver is the easiest way to see the Grand Mosque, the Louvre and the Presidential Palace in one day and be back in Dubai for dinner. Book an hourly chauffeur from around eight in the morning and the car stays with you the whole day, so there is no waiting for taxis between sights. Allow around 90 minutes each way on Sheikh Zayed Road and eight to ten hours in total.

What does a Dubai to Abu Dhabi day trip look like at a glance?

What should I have ready before the day?

A day trip goes wrong in the planning, not on the road. Sort these the night before and the day itself runs on rails.

  • Your pickup address in Dubai written out with the building name, and a pickup time, ideally between 7.30am and 8.30am
  • Timed entry tickets for the Louvre and Qasr Al Watan booked online, so you are not in a queue at the door
  • Your mosque booking made on the mosque's own website, which Experience Abu Dhabi recommends for ease of entry
  • Loose, covering clothing for the mosque: long sleeves, long trousers or a long skirt, and a headscarf for women
  • A working phone with roaming or an eSIM so your chauffeur can reach you when you come out of each sight
  • A rough order of stops agreed with your chauffeur at pickup, with the mosque first and the Corniche or Saadiyat last
  • Child seats requested on the booking if you are travelling with small children
  • Water and sunscreen, because the walk across the mosque courtyard is long and there is no shade

How long does the drive from Dubai to Abu Dhabi take?

Around 90 minutes from central Dubai to the Grand Mosque, which sits on the Dubai side of Abu Dhabi and is the first sight you reach. From Dubai Marina or JBR it is a little less, from Deira and the DXB side a little more. The distance is roughly 130 km, and almost all of it is fast dual carriageway.

The road is Sheikh Zayed Road, which becomes the E11 and runs in a straight line past Jebel Ali and Ghantoot to the Abu Dhabi border. Your chauffeur will pick between the E11 and the inland Sheikh Mohammed bin Zayed Road (E311) depending on where you start and what the traffic is doing. From Downtown or Business Bay on a weekday morning, the E311 can save a fair amount of time.

Leaving Dubai before 8am on a weekday means sitting in the outbound rush along the Marina and Jebel Ali. Leaving at 8.30am puts you behind most of it, and you still arrive at the mosque by 10am. Coming back, the evening rush into Abu Dhabi does not affect you because you are heading out, but expect slow traffic from Jebel Ali into Dubai between 5pm and 7pm.

Should I book an hourly chauffeur or two one-way transfers?

Book the hourly service for a proper day out and two transfers only if you plan to stay in one place all day. The hourly chauffeur in Dubai gives you the driver and the car for the whole day with unlimited stops, so you move between the mosque, the Louvre, the palace and lunch without booking anything else. The car is your base for bags, water, and the jackets you take off after the mosque.

Two one-way transfers make sense when you are going for a single event, a meeting on Al Maryah Island, or a full day at Yas Island. A Dubai to Abu Dhabi transfer drops you at the door in the morning and a second booking brings you back at a set time. Between the two, you are on your own for local transport.

For an eight to ten hour day covering three sights, the hourly booking is the simpler option and the one I would take every time. Book it from the pickup time in Dubai to the drop-off time back in Dubai, and let your chauffeur handle the rest.

What is a realistic one-day Abu Dhabi itinerary from Dubai?

Three sights is the right number for a day trip: the Grand Mosque, the Louvre and Qasr Al Watan. Add a drive along the Corniche and lunch, and you are back in Dubai by around 7pm. Trying to fit in Yas Island as well turns the day into a rush.

Morning: Sheikh Zayed Grand Mosque

Start at the mosque, because it is the first thing you reach coming from Dubai and it is at its quietest early. There is no fee to enter, and the same page notes that respectful clothing is required and that the main prayer hall is closed to visitors on Fridays between 12pm and 3pm for Friday prayers. If you are going on a Friday, arrive by 10am or plan the mosque for the late afternoon.

Give yourself 90 minutes. Experience Abu Dhabi describes free guided tours in Arabic and English, and they are worth joining for the detail on the calligraphy and the 82 domes. The mosque is still a working place of worship that welcomes up to 50,000 worshippers a day, so follow the signage and the dress code without complaint.

Late morning: Louvre Abu Dhabi

From the mosque it is around 25 minutes across the city to Saadiyat Island. The Louvre sits in the Saadiyat Cultural District and covers 9,200 square metres of permanent and temporary galleries, so two hours is enough for the highlights without rushing. Experience Abu Dhabi lists free entry for children under 18, which helps if you are travelling as a family.

Book your ticket online before the day and pick a late-morning slot. The museum's Children's Museum is included in the ticket, and the dome's famous "rain of light" is at its best around midday when the sun is directly overhead.

Lunch and the Corniche

Your chauffeur can drop you at a restaurant on Saadiyat or on the Corniche, and the car waits nearby. This is the part of the day where a private driver earns their keep, because you are not hunting for a taxi with a full stomach at 2pm in the heat. Ask for a slow drive along the Corniche after lunch to see the skyline from the water side.

Afternoon: Qasr Al Watan

Qasr Al Watan, the Presidential Palace, is at Al Ras Al Akhdar at the western end of the Corniche and is the natural last stop. Experience Abu Dhabi lists tickets at AED 65 for adults and AED 30 for children, with entry through the Visitor Centre. Allow 90 minutes for the halls, the library and the House of Knowledge.

If you want to see the Palace in Motion light show, which the same page says runs nightly from 8pm, you will be back in Dubai late. It is a good option if your group is happy with a 10pm return, and the hourly booking simply runs on. Otherwise leave the palace by 5pm and you are home in time for dinner.

What does a private driver for the day cost, and what is included?

The hourly chauffeur service starts from AED 150 per hour, and an Abu Dhabi day out is priced by the hour from your Dubai pickup to your Dubai drop-off. The exact figure depends on the vehicle you pick, and the booking form on the hourly chauffeur page shows it before you pay. There is no surge pricing and no charge for sitting in traffic.

Every Emirates Limo price is all-inclusive. Salik and Darb tolls, VAT and any other taxes are built into the fixed price, and nothing is collected in the car. Fuel, the chauffeur's time and waiting between stops are all covered by the hourly rate.

The tolls themselves are worth knowing about so you are not surprised by the gantries. Salik is Dubai's automatic toll system, run by the Roads and Transport Authority, and you pass at least one gate on the way out of the city. Abu Dhabi's Darb gates sit on the bridges onto the island, and Abu Dhabi Mobility charges AED 4 per crossing between 7am and 9am and between 3pm and 7pm, with no charge on Sundays and official holidays.

Payment is online by card with an instant email confirmation. Cancel 24 hours or more before pickup for a full refund. Inside 24 hours, and for no-shows, the booking is charged in full, so if the weather or your plans look uncertain, make the call the day before.

Which vehicle should I book for a day trip to Abu Dhabi?

A sedan for up to three or four people, an SUV or van for five or six. The fleet page has the full seat and luggage counts, but the short version is that the Lexus ES300 takes four passengers and the BMW 7-Series and Mercedes-Benz S-Class take three each. All three are comfortable for three hours on the motorway across the day.

For a family or a group of friends, the GMC Yukon and the Mercedes-Benz V-Class each take six passengers, and the Kia Carnival takes five. The van is the better pick for a day out because everyone can face each other and the boot swallows the bags, coats and shopping you collect along the way. Child seats are available on request when you book, so add them to the booking rather than asking on the day.

If the group is larger than six, book two cars rather than squeezing. Both chauffeurs follow the same itinerary and the second car is a fixed price as well.

What goes wrong on Dubai to Abu Dhabi day trips?

Turning up at the mosque in the wrong clothes. The dress code is strict and enforced at the entrance, so wear long, loose clothing that covers arms and legs, and women should bring a scarf for their hair. Check the mosque's own guidance the night before rather than guessing.

Arriving at the mosque at Friday lunchtime. Experience Abu Dhabi is clear that the main prayer hall is closed to visitors between 12pm and 3pm on Fridays. Go in the morning or swap the order and finish at the mosque as the sun goes down, which is when the building looks its best anyway.

Not booking timed tickets. The Louvre and Qasr Al Watan both sell tickets online, and a slot booked in advance skips the queue at the door. On a public holiday or a winter weekend, the walk-up queue at the Louvre can eat half an hour of your day.

Trying to do Yas Island as well. Yas is on the far side of the city from the mosque and the theme parks need a full day each. Either make Yas the whole trip, with a private car from Dubai to Abu Dhabi in each direction, or leave it for another day.

Setting off in the morning rush. A 7am pickup from Downtown puts you in the thick of outbound traffic past the Marina and Jebel Ali. Leave at 8.30am and you arrive at the mosque within a few minutes of the early starters, with far less time sat on the E11.

Booking two transfers and then wanting to change the return time. A one-way transfer has a fixed pickup time and the chauffeur is committed to it. If your day might run long, book by the hour instead, where the car simply stays with you until you are done.

Cancelling late. The refund rule is 24 hours: cancel before that and you get everything back, cancel after it and you do not. Sandstorms and heavy rain are rare, but if the forecast looks bad, decide the evening before.

Can I do the trip in reverse, from Abu Dhabi to Dubai?

Yes, and it works the same way. Emirates Limo runs a chauffeur service in Abu Dhabi by the hour or the full day, and a door-to-door Abu Dhabi to Dubai transfer for a one-way trip to the Burj Khalifa, the Dubai Mall or the Palm. The same all-inclusive pricing, the same 24-hour cancellation rule and the same fleet apply in both directions.

For getting about inside Abu Dhabi without a driver, Experience Abu Dhabi's getting around page lists the alternatives: taxis, public buses, the Yas Express shuttle and bike sharing. With a chauffeur for the day you will not need any of them, but it is useful to know what is there if you split off from the group for an hour.
